claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations and spatial heterogeneity.
A graph-based machine-learning model can explicitly encode the alloy’s local chemical environments and hierarchical structural features at multiple length scales.
Explicitly encoding the hierarchical heterostructure will improve prediction accuracy for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness relative to prior approaches.
The graph-based model will be more computationally efficient than thermophysical-parameter calculations, CALPHAD, first-principles calculations, and conventional machine learning.
Graph-based machine-learning models can capture complex spatial relationships and chemical environments in hierarchical alloys.
Capturing spatial relationships and chemical environments enables direct mapping from microstructure to mechanical properties.
The proposed direct microstructure-to-property mapping bypasses exhaustive thermophysical calculations and first-principles simulations.
Prediction errors for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness will be at least 30% lower than those of the baseline methods.
Computational time per prediction will be reduced by at least a factor of 10 relative to the baseline methods.
The model will cease to be reliable when the hierarchical heterostructure is poorly characterized.
The model will cease to be reliable for compositions or microstructures outside the training distribution, including new phases, extreme disorder, or uncharacterized defects.
Sparse or noisy microstructural and mechanical-property data may reduce the predicted accuracy improvement.
A blinded held-out benchmark can compare the graph model and baseline models using RMSE or MAE and computational time per prediction.
Failure to obtain both at least 30% lower prediction error and at least 10-fold faster prediction on the held-out set will falsify the hypothesis.
